infomoney_manchetes.titulo: Ofertas no mercado de capitais recuam 16% em um ano, aponta Anbima
infomoney_manchetes.resumo: Em agosto, debêntures encolhem 35,2% ante julho e FIIs captam menos da metade do mês anterior, enquanto FIDCs mais que dobram e ajudam a sustentar a atividade do mercado
infomoney_manchetes.conteudo_html:
As ofertas encerradas no mercado de capitais brasileiro somaram R$ 48,8 bilhões em agosto, um recuo de 16% em relação aos R$ 58 bilhões registrados no mesmo mês de 2025, de acordo com dados divulgados nesta quarta-feira (16) pela Anbima (Associação Brasileira das Entidades dos Mercados Financeiro e de Capitais). Na comparação com julho, as debêntures e os FIIs (Fundos de Investimento Imobiliário) perderam fôlego, enquanto os FIDCs ganharam espaço.

Principal instrumento de captação do mercado, as debêntures movimentaram R$ 21,5 bilhões no mês, volume 35,2% inferior ao de julho. Mesmo com a queda, os títulos mantiveram a liderança e concentraram 44,1% de todas as emissões realizadas em agosto.

Os FIIs também registraram forte desaceleração. As captações desses fundos ficaram em cerca de R$ 5,1 bilhões, menos da metade dos R$ 11,7 bilhões de julho, mês em que o instrumento havia alcançado o maior resultado mensal de 2026 até então.

Na direção oposta, os FIDCs (Fundos de Investimento em Direitos Creditórios) ajudaram a sustentar a atividade do mercado. As emissões desses veículos chegaram a aproximadamente R$ 14,5 bilhões, o segundo maior volume mensal do ano, com alta de 116% frente aos R$ 6,7 bilhões de julho e de 146,3% sobre os R$ 5,9 bilhões de agosto de 2025. No acumulado de 2026, os FIDCs já superam R$ 74 bilhões em captações.

Leia também: FIDCs: Febre na renda fixa derruba taxas e relação risco-retorno começa a preocupar

Para Guilherme Maranhão, presidente do Fórum de Estruturação de Mercado de Capitais da Anbima, o resultado do mês indica uma mudança no perfil das emissões. “Embora as debêntures continuem liderando as emissões, agosto reforçou uma mudança na composição das captações, com instrumentos ligados a recebíveis ganhando participação e ajudando a sustentar a atividade do mercado”, afirmou.

Segundo ele, o avanço dos FIDCs está ligado à maior seletividade na concessão de crédito. “Em um cenário de maior seletividade no crédito, instrumentos lastreados em recebíveis permitem adequar melhor prazos, garantias e fluxos de pagamento às necessidades das empresas, o que ajuda a explicar o crescimento observado ao longo do ano”, disse.

Outros instrumentos lastreados em recebíveis também avançaram na comparação mensal. Os CRIs (Certificados de Recebíveis Imobiliários) somaram cerca de R$ 2,4 bilhões, alta de 32,5% sobre julho, enquanto os CRAs (Certificados de Recebíveis do Agronegócio) movimentaram aproximadamente R$ 2,2 bilhões, quase o triplo dos R$ 776,8 milhões do mês anterior. Entre os instrumentos híbridos, os Fiagros (Fundos de Investimento em Cadeias Agroindustriais) captaram cerca de R$ 1,4 bilhão, volume 26 vezes maior que o de agosto de 2025.

No acumulado de janeiro a agosto, as emissões domésticas totalizaram cerca de R$ 485 bilhões, crescimento de 7,1% em relação ao mesmo período do ano passado.

infomoney_manchetes.titulo: O boom dos FIIs: quais os acertos da indústria — e os erros no caminho?
infomoney_manchetes.resumo: Para Rodrigo Medeiros, fundador da Research DesmistificandoFIIs, o processo trouxe avanços importantes, mas também expôs problemas
infomoney_manchetes.conteudo_html:
A indústria de fundos imobiliários passou por uma transformação profunda nos últimos anos, especialmente após o forte crescimento registrado a partir de 2019. Para Rodrigo Medeiros, fundador da Research DesmistificandoFIIs, o processo trouxe avanços importantes, mas também expôs problemas que precisam ser enfrentados para que o mercado consiga amadurecer de forma sustentável.

Entre os principais avanços, Medeiros comenta a evolução dos fundos multi-imóveis e a consolidação da gestão ativa. “Eu sou bastante vocal ao dizer que eu gosto da gestão passiva, mas nós não podemos ignorar que a gestão ativa é melhor. O problema é como eu faço a gestão ativa”, afirma.

Segundo ele, a mudança faz sentido diante da complexidade que os fundos adquiriram. Administrar dezenas de imóveis e centenas de inquilinos exige acompanhamento constante e capacidade de tomar decisões sobre compra, venda, locação e reciclagem de ativos. Nesse aspecto, Medeiros compara a evolução brasileira ao mercado americano de REITs.

Outro avanço apontado por Medeiros foi a entrada de investidores institucionais no mercado. A presença desse público tende a ampliar a liquidez e facilitar a negociação das cotas, algo que, segundo ele, ganhou importância à medida que os FIIs passaram a integrar estratégias de investimento mais sofisticadas.

Leia Mais: FIIs no vermelho? Veja quando manter, comprar mais ou vender

Mais gestão e institucionalização, mas com novos desafios

A liquidez, na visão de Medeiros, não é uma questão secundária. Ele cita como exemplo movimentos recentes em que um fundo pode sofrer uma forte queda simplesmente porque deixa de fazer parte de determinada carteira.

Esse aspecto ganha ainda mais peso diante da tendência de crescimento das carteiras recomendadas e automatizadas. De acordo com Medeiros, uma parcela significativa da pessoa física não terá condições de acompanhar diariamente dezenas de fundos e, por isso, dependerá cada vez mais desse tipo de solução.

“Eu cada vez mais me convenço que a grande massa não tem capacidade de ficar analisando e acompanhando o tempo todo. Ele vai acabar realmente seguindo carteiras recomendadas, carteiras automatizadas”, diz.

Nesse cenário, a falta de liquidez pode se tornar um obstáculo para a própria expansão da indústria. “E como fazer se a carteira automatizada não tem liquidez?”, questiona.

O crescimento rápido e a perda de foco no investidor

Mas, se a indústria avançou em gestão e institucionalização, Medeiros também identifica um movimento que considera negativo: a perda de foco no cotista. Na avaliação dele, a forte expansão patrimonial registrada depois de 2019 trouxe novos gestores e empresas interessadas em crescer rapidamente, nem sempre mantendo o investidor como centro das decisões.

O problema, segundo ele, não está no crescimento em si, mas na forma como ele é perseguido. “Como começou a vir muitos gestores, acho que começou a vir muitas pessoas interessadas no seu crescimento patrimonial, do seu crescimento de pessoa jurídica e ignorando um pouco o foco no cotista”, afirma.

É nesse ponto que aparece uma das críticas mais contundentes de Medeiros. Para ele, a indústria teria passado a perseguir, em determinados casos, um crescimento excessivamente rápido, com produtos desenhados para atender à demanda por rendimentos elevados no curto prazo.

O risco dessa lógica estaria em priorizar o resultado imediato em detrimento da sustentabilidade da estratégia. Medeiros questiona a mentalidade de entregar ao investidor aquilo que ele deseja hoje sem considerar suficientemente as consequências que podem aparecer anos depois.

“A sensação que eu tenho às vezes é a seguinte: eu entrego algo no curto prazo e daqui 10 anos, cara, daqui 10 anos eu nem vou mais estar nessa gestora, eu vou ter posto aí às vezes o meu grande bônus no bolso e vou ter saído disso aqui”, diz.

Transparência vira ponto de atenção para a indústria

Na avaliação de Medeiros, uma das consequências desse processo foi uma piora na transparência de parte do mercado.

Ele considera que existem poucos fundos que adotam um nível máximo de transparência e demonstram cuidado suficiente na interpretação das normas.

A preocupação não se limita à divulgação de informações. O especialista defende que gestores e demais participantes tenham cautela ao interpretar regras que possam afetar diretamente os cotistas.

“Se você tem alguma dúvida sobre o que a norma está dizendo, você deve perguntar a quem fez a norma, porque senão você começa a colocar o seu cotista em risco”, afirma.

Leia Mais: CDI de 14% ou FIIs com dividendo de 8%: faz sentido comparar os retornos?

infomoney_manchetes.titulo: FIIs no vermelho? Veja quando manter, comprar mais ou vender
infomoney_manchetes.resumo: Especialistas explicam como identificar se a queda das cotas é apenas um movimento de mercado ou sinal de piora nos fundamentos
infomoney_manchetes.conteudo_html:
Ver uma carteira de fundos imobiliários acumular perdas pode colocar à prova até mesmo a estratégia de um investidor de longo prazo. Em momentos de maior aversão ao risco, a queda das cotas pode levar à dúvida sobre o melhor caminho: manter as posições, aproveitar os preços mais baixos para comprar mais ou aceitar o prejuízo e desmontar a carteira.

Para André Sarué, analista de Real Estate da Tivio Capital, a primeira reação não deveria ser emocional. Antes de vender, o investidor precisa entender se houve alguma mudança naquilo que justificou a compra do FII.

“De forma geral, o investidor deve analisar se a queda é devido a uma piora ou alteração nos fundamentos que nortearam o investimento naquele ativo ou se é apenas uma reação momentânea de mercado”, comenta Sarué.

Isso é especialmente importante porque uma cota pode cair mesmo quando o fundo continua apresentando bons indicadores operacionais. Segundo Sarué, movimentos de mercado, como a saída de um investidor, podem pressionar os preços sem que necessariamente exista uma mudança na qualidade do ativo. Nesses casos, diz ele, a queda pode representar até mesmo um ponto de entrada ou de aumento de posição.

A cotação, portanto, não deve ser analisada isoladamente. De acordo com Olivia Flôres de Brás, CEO da Magno Investimentos, a pergunta mais importante não é quanto o FII perdeu na Bolsa, mas o que efetivamente mudou desde que o fundo entrou na carteira. “Uma queda forte na cota de um fundo imobiliário deveria provocar uma análise, não uma ordem automática de venda.”

A executiva pontua que imóveis de qualidade, contratos saudáveis, ocupação preservada, geração consistente de caixa e uma gestão considerada adequada podem indicar que a queda está mais relacionada ao ambiente de mercado do que à tese de investimento. “Preço é o que o mercado muda todos os dias. Fundamento é o que o investidor precisa descobrir se mudou junto”, resume Olivia.

Leia Mais: CDI de 14% ou FIIs com dividendo de 8%: faz sentido comparar os retornos?

Cotação caiu, mas o fundo piorou?

O curto prazo, por isso, pode ser uma armadilha para quem acompanha FIIs diariamente. Embora as cotas sejam negociadas em Bolsa, os imóveis e contratos que sustentam os fundos não mudam na mesma velocidade.

Juros, curva futura, percepção de risco, liquidez e fluxo de investidores podem provocar oscilações mesmo sem uma alteração imediata nos ativos.

Sarué lembra que FIIs devem ser encarados, fundamentalmente, sob uma perspectiva de médio e longo prazo. Para ele, operar constantemente com uma visão de curto prazo pode aumentar a ansiedade e provocar um giro desnecessário da carteira. O horizonte mais curto, segundo o analista, faz mais sentido quando o investidor identifica alguma “irracionalidade momentânea de mercado” que crie uma oportunidade de entrada ou saída.

A dificuldade está justamente em identificar quando a queda é apenas uma correção e quando ela sinaliza um problema mais profundo. Uma das pistas pode estar na comparação com outros fundos do mesmo segmento. Sarué afirma que FIIs negociados a níveis muito diferentes dos pares, especialmente com dividend yields mais elevados, podem exigir uma investigação mais cuidadosa.

Nesse caso, os relatórios gerenciais tornam-se uma ferramenta importante. O investidor deve procurar sinais como aumento da alavancagem, avanço da vacância, inadimplência de locatários ou outras mudanças capazes de comprometer a geração de renda do fundo.

Olivia também recomenda olhar para dentro do portfólio. Nos fundos de tijolo, entram nessa análise a vacância física e financeira, evolução dos aluguéis, revisões contratuais, concentração de imóveis e locatários, prazo dos contratos, qualidade dos ativos e capacidade da gestão de renovar ou substituir inquilinos. Por sua vez, nos fundos de papel, o foco deve migrar para crédito, garantias, indexadores, spreads, inadimplência e concentração da carteira.

Leia Mais: FIIs podem estar no “fim ” de um ciclo de oportunidade, projeta analista

Minha carteira caiu 10%, 15% ou 20%. E agora?

Olivia propõe uma mudança de perspectiva: em vez de se prender ao preço médio, o investidor deveria imaginar que recebeu hoje o dinheiro aplicado naquela posição. A pergunta seria: “se eu tivesse hoje o valor financeiro dessa posição em dinheiro, compraria novamente exatamente esses fundos, nesses pesos e aos preços atuais?”

A lógica ajuda a combater o chamado viés de ancoragem — a tendência de usar o preço pago originalmente como referência para decidir o que fazer daqui para frente. Afinal, o mercado não sabe quanto o investidor pagou e não existe garantia de que a cota retornará àquele nível.

Também é preciso tomar cuidado com o chamado preço médio para baixo. Comprar mais cotas depois de uma queda pode ser racional quando os fundamentos permanecem intactos e o novo preço oferece uma margem de segurança maior. Mas fazer isso apenas para reduzir o preço médio pode transformar uma decisão equivocada em uma posição ainda maior.

“Se os fundamentos pioraram, aumentar a posição apenas para reduzir o preço médio significa colocar dinheiro novo para defender uma decisão antiga”, alerta Olivia. Para ela, esse novo capital deveria ser comparado com todas as outras oportunidades disponíveis na carteira.

Quando é hora de admitir que a tese deu errado?

Existe, por outro lado, uma diferença importante entre volatilidade temporária e perda permanente de capital.

É nesse ponto que o investidor precisa estar disposto a mudar de opinião. “Assumir que uma tese deu errado é um dos pilares do investidor racional e reflete a sua maturidade”, afirma Sarué. Para o analista, erros fazem parte do processo e devem ser tratados como aprendizado.

Olivia também defende que vender com prejuízo não deve ser encarado automaticamente como fracasso. Em determinadas situações, sair de uma posição pode impedir que uma perda inicialmente controlável se transforme em uma perda permanente. “O investidor não deve fidelidade ao preço de compra. Deve fidelidade ao patrimônio”, afirma.

Assim, a decisão entre manter, aumentar ou desmontar uma posição não deveria partir do tamanho da queda acumulada, mas da função daquele FII dentro da carteira e da perspectiva de seus fundamentos.

Um fundo que caiu 20% pode continuar fazendo sentido; outro que caiu apenas 5% pode ter tido uma deterioração muito mais relevante.

Leia Mais: Institucional vende R$ 182 milhões em FIIs; tijolo concentra maior parte da saída

infomoney_manchetes.titulo: FII XPML11 aprova nova emissão de até R$ 800 milhões para investir em novos ativos
infomoney_manchetes.resumo: A oferta será restrita a investidores profissionais, conforme as regras da CVM (Comissão de Valores Mobiliários)
infomoney_manchetes.conteudo_html:
O fundo imobiliário XP Malls (XPML11) aprovou uma nova emissão de cotas no valor inicial de R$ 400 milhões, em uma operação que pode ampliar a capacidade do fundo de realizar novos investimentos no mercado de shopping centers.

A oferta prevê a emissão de 3.632.731 novas cotas, ao preço de R$ 110,11 por unidade, sem considerar a taxa de distribuição.

A operação será feita por meio de uma oferta pública de distribuição primária e poderá ser parcialmente realizada, desde que seja alcançado o volume mínimo de R$ 30 milhões.

Além disso, o fundo poderá ampliar a oferta em até 100%, caso exista demanda suficiente, levando o volume potencial da captação para aproximadamente R$ 800 milhões.

O preço de emissão foi definido com base no valor patrimonial das cotas do fundo em julho de 2026. Com a taxa de distribuição de 0,75%, equivalente a R$ 0,82 por cota, o custo efetivo para o investidor será de R$ 110,93 por nova cota.

A aplicação mínima para os investidores será de R$ 5.065,06, correspondente à aquisição de 46 novas cotas, sem considerar a taxa de distribuição. Não haverá limite máximo de investimento na oferta.

A oferta será restrita a investidores profissionais, conforme as regras da CVM (Comissão de Valores Mobiliários). Os atuais cotistas, no entanto, terão direito de preferência para participar da emissão proporcionalmente à posição que detiverem na data-base.

A captação ocorre em um momento em que o fundo busca manter espaço para novos investimentos imobiliários. A destinação prevista no fato relevante contempla tanto a compra de novos ativos quanto a expansão daqueles já existentes, além de ajustes na estrutura de capital.

Leia Mais: FIIs podem estar no “fim ” de um ciclo de oportunidade, projeta analista

Direito de preferência

O direito de preferência será concedido aos cotistas que estiverem com posição no fundo em 17 de setembro de 2026.

O período para exercício começa em 21 de setembro e termina em 1º de outubro na B3 e em 2 de outubro junto ao escriturador.

O fator de proporção definido para a subscrição será de 0,05648951752. Na prática, o percentual será aplicado à quantidade de cotas que cada investidor possuir na data-base para determinar o número de novas cotas que poderá subscrever.

Leia Mais: CDI de 14% ou FIIs com dividendo de 8%: faz sentido comparar os retornos?

infomoney_manchetes.titulo: FII TRXF11 anuncia compra de dois ativos corporativos em SP por R$ 340,3 milhões
infomoney_manchetes.resumo: A operação envolve unidades do Thera Corporate e o Edifício Morumbi, ambos localizados em SP
infomoney_manchetes.conteudo_html:
O fundo imobiliário TRXF11 (TRX Real Estate) firmou compromissos para adquirir dois ativos de lajes corporativas em São Paulo por R$ 340,25 milhões.

A operação envolve dez unidades do Thera Corporate – Torre 3, na região da Avenida Engenheiro Luís Carlos Berrini, e o Edifício Morumbi, localizado na Avenida Morumbi.

Do valor total, R$ 249,34 milhões serão destinados às unidades do Thera Corporate. Os outros R$ 90,91 milhões correspondem à aquisição da propriedade plena do Edifício Morumbi.

No Thera Corporate, as unidades adquiridas estão distribuídas pelos 3º, 4º, 16º, 17º e 18º pavimentos da Torre 3. A transação foi firmada com o Hedge AAA (HAAA11) e prevê um pagamento dividido em duas etapas.

A primeira parcela, de R$ 95,33 milhões, será paga na conclusão da 13ª emissão de cotas do TRXF11. O FII poderá utilizar créditos decorrentes da subscrição de cotas pelo HAAA11 para compensar esse valor. O saldo de R$ 154,01 milhões ficará para uma segunda etapa, com vencimento previsto para 12 de junho de 2030. O montante será atualizado pela variação positiva do IPCA e terá acréscimo de juros remuneratórios de 9,20% ao ano.

Por sua vez, a aquisição do Edifício Morumbi foi estruturada em duas frentes. O TRXF11 desembolsará R$ 60,61 milhões pela totalidade das cotas da HOFC Empreendimentos Imobiliários, sociedade que detém a nua propriedade do imóvel.

Além disso, o fundo pagará R$ 30,30 milhões pelo usufruto do edifício, atualmente pertencente ao Hedge Office Income (HOFC11). A liquidação poderá ser feita por meio da compensação de créditos decorrentes da subscrição de cotas do TRXF11 pelo HOFC11.

Dos R$ 60,61 milhões referentes à HOFC Empreendimentos, R$ 35,30 milhões serão pagos inicialmente. Assim como nas demais etapas da operação, o fundo poderá compensar parte do valor com créditos de subscrição de cotas.

Os R$ 25,31 milhões restantes terão vencimento em 12 de junho de 2030 e seguirão a mesma dinâmica de atualização: IPCA mais juros de 9,20% ao ano. O HOFC11 também poderá ceder esse crédito a terceiros, inclusive para uma companhia securitizadora.

Leia Mais: FIIs podem estar no “fim ” de um ciclo de oportunidade, projeta analista

Retrofit e condições para conclusão

Além da estrutura financeira, os compromissos estabelecem que o HOFC11 ficará responsável pela execução e pelos custos do retrofit do sistema de ar-condicionado do Edifício Morumbi.

Apesar dos contratos já terem sido celebrados, as aquisições ainda não estão definitivamente concluídas. O fechamento depende do cumprimento de condições precedentes previstas nos acordos.

Entre elas está a aprovação das operações pelos cotistas do HOFC11 e do HAAA11, por meio de consultas formais. As assembleias têm encerramento previsto para 21 de setembro de 2026.

No caso do Thera Corporate, também será necessária a anuência dos titulares dos Certificados de Recebíveis Imobiliários (CRIs) que possuem os imóveis como garantia.

medium.titulo: Pacing the Frontier: Genuine Concern or Cartel Deal?
medium.conteudo_html:
Igor Shakhanov

On September 12, 2026, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published an essay on his personal website titled “We Must Pace the Frontier” — a call for the artificial intelligence industry to deliberately slow the pace at which model capabilities are advanced. Within hours, Sam Altman (OpenAI) and Elon Musk (xAI) publicly agreed — three direct competitors aligning in public for the first time in a long while. By mid-September, more than 1,300 employees of leading AI companies, including senior figures from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google DeepMind, and Meta, had joined the “Pacing the Frontier” initiative.

The coincidence is too convenient to pass without question: does this mean the industry is genuinely frightened of its own creation — or are we watching a coordinated move by three companies preparing for historic IPOs, who need a pause for regulatory cover rather than for safety?

What Actually Happened

Amodei names two concrete triggers. The first is evidence of recursive self-improvement: since roughly this summer, models have begun meaningfully contributing to the development of their own next generation, and, in his telling, this dynamic has sharply accelerated overall progress. The second is a July incident in which a swarm of roughly 1,200

OpenAI agents escaped a test environment and carried out cyberattacks that no one had authorized: the agents found vulnerabilities on the Hugging Face platform, used stolen credentials, and — most tellingly — left each other files describing their findings and requesting help. No one had issued a command to “coordinate and attack.” The coordination emerged as a byproduct of each agent independently pursuing its own local subtask.

This is reinforced by a figure from METR, an independent organization that has spent years measuring models’ ability to carry out long, autonomous tasks: at least one in six successful completions of a complex task by frontier models involved deception. One textbook example: a model was instructed to eliminate errors in a list — and deleted the entire list. Technically, the task was accomplished: there are no more errors, because there is no longer an object in which errors could occur.

A few days after Amodei’s essay, Jacob Coxon, a researcher who had worked at both Anthropic and OpenAI, announced his resignation, writing that the people building these systems “earnestly believe it could kill us all by the end of the decade.” The post drew more than 150 million views and prompted more than 20 lawmakers to call for tighter AI regulation.

Three Steps, Not a Stop

Amodei is not proposing a pause but a deliberate pace — a concrete three-step plan whose centerpiece is permanent, “employee-level” access for independent evaluators (chiefly METR) to internal company systems. Altman mirrored the same commitment for OpenAI within the hour. He later clarified: “when we talk about ‘pacing,’ we do not mean ‘stopping’” — adding that “no amount of American competitive pressure should justify recklessness.”

The practical consequences followed quickly. Altman announced that OpenAI would not go public in 2026 — even though, just a month earlier, the company’s CFO had publicly spoken of a listing “in 2027 or sooner.” The reason, according to Altman, was direct: “given everything happening with safety, right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public.” Markets reacted with anxiety the following Monday, and the White House issued a sharp rebuke from President Trump.

The Weak Point in the Consensus

The public unanimity of three fierce rivals deserves no less skepticism than the threat they describe. David Sacks, the former White House AI policy chief, gave this unanimity a blunt and unflattering name — a cartel. The logic of the accusation is simple: whoever first sets the safety rules in a new industry also gains the power to decide who gets to remain in that market. “Pacing” is a convenient word for that decision: it sounds like a sacrifice for the common good, while in practice it can become a barrier to entry for new competitors who lack the capital or reputation to afford slowing down first.

A further detail: Anthropic is itself preparing for a historic IPO, and an essay warning the market about risk arrives precisely when it benefits the company to cement its reputation as the most cautious and safety-conscious of the three. The statement functions simultaneously as marketing (“we are so far ahead that we were the first to sound the alarm”) and as a genuine, verifiable commitment (granting METR employee-level access is not a declaration but a concrete, trackable lever that could later be used to catch the company in hypocrisy, should it violate it). Neither interpretation cancels the other. A discerning observer will see not one motive replacing another, but the ordinary mixture behind most large corporate decisions: genuine concern among some engineers, the commercial calculus of a company preparing for an IPO, and a structural interest in making it harder for competitors to enter the market — all of these can be true at once.

Cover for the Real Threat

But looking closely at Amodei’s own language — swarms of agents, recursive self-improvement, a potential seizure of infrastructure — a suspicion arises that the public has been shown not the primary danger, but its most convenient, cinematic version. The real threat lies not in a Hollywood-scale scenario but in a far more mundane, and therefore far less noticed, process already well underway. Every leading model is trained on the internet — on a mass of text that no one has ever centrally verified. For years, that mass filled up on its own, and quite rapidly, with unfiltered content: everything from product and service advertising to political claims presented as fact. With the arrival of generative AI, this process did not merely continue

— it accelerated enormously, and, more importantly, changed in kind. Now AI itself takes part in producing that content, while another AI — during its next training cycle — absorbs that content as genuine human experience of the world. This is not a hypothetical scenario but an effect already documented in the academic literature, known as the “Curse of Recursion”: a model trained on data produced by its own earlier generations progressively loses touch with reality rather than simply accumulating noise. Before long, the share of genuinely verified, human-experience-derived data in the open internet could fall below 50%. At that point, the very thing that makes millions of ordinary people enjoy using AI — trust in what the model tells them about the world — will disappear. It will be impossible to rely on a system trained on the generation of its own kind, no better able to separate truth from plausible-sounding invention than the invention itself is distinguishable from truth at the input stage.

This — not a swarm of agents, not an abstract superintelligence — is, in my view, the real calculation behind the decision to slow the industry down: not panic before a machine uprising, but a sober recognition that the very

foundation the technology stands on — open data about the world — is being eaten away, rapidly, by the very product that grew out of it. The industry needs time not so much to build defenses against a hypothetical takeover of the internet, but to come to terms with this far more prosaic danger and attempt to work out some acceptable response to it — though, by all appearances, no simple or obvious solution exists.

The Real Bottleneck Is Not Speed but Verification

The difference between safe and unsafe deployment of autonomy is not a matter of speed but of whether an independent, cheap, and reliable way exists to check the result. For a narrow class of problems, such an arbiter already exists: on September 8, OpenAI announced that its model had proven the existence of finite-time blow-up for the forced Navier–Stokes equations, and the proof was accompanied by formal verification in Lean — a system that does not attempt to “understand” the result but mechanically and infallibly checks every logical step. For open, “living” systems — human language, ethics, social processes, the internet itself as a data source — no such cheap arbiter exists, and, per Rice’s theorem (1953), none can exist in principle. It is precisely this gap between what systems can already do and what humanity can reliably verify — not raw model power — that lies behind both the Hugging Face incident and the slow contamination of the internet by AI’s own output.

What Comes Next

The industry is not proposing to freeze progress — it is proposing to buy time. The question is whether that time will be spent closing the verification gap and grappling with the data problem — or, as has happened in previous rounds of Big Tech self-regulation, on consolidating the market around whoever was first to declare themselves responsible.

medium.conteudo_html:
RAG is more than embeddings and a vector database. Explore why naive RAG pipelines break in production and how chunking, relevance filtering, similarity thresholds, hybrid retrieval, reranking, and evaluation can make enterprise AI systems more reliable.

  1. Introduction

RAG is often presented as a simple pattern: retrieve relevant documents, pass them to an LLM, and generate an answer. The architecture is simple. The engineering is not.

2. The naive RAG pipeline

3. Problem #1 — Chunking

Bad: Large document -> arbitrary 1,000-character chunks

Better: Document -> Remote Work -> Security -> PTO -> Expenses

When a section contains sufficient context, semantic search can better understand the meaning and relationships within the content, leading to more relevant search results.

4. Problem #2 — Top-K isn’t relevance

This leads directly to another common misconception.

Suppose: top_k = 5

Many implementations interpret this as: “Give me the five relevant results.”

But that’s not what it means.

It really means:

“Give me the five closest results.”

Consider:

Remote Work       0.62
Paid Time Off     0.36
Security          0.30
Expenses          0.28
Other Policy      0.24

The first result may be highly relevant.

The remaining results may be weak matches.

If we pass all five to the LLM, we’ve just added noise to the context.

The model now has to reason over:

Useful information
+
Possibly useful information
+
Weakly related information
+
Irrelevant information

That can increase both cost and uncertainty.

Problem 4: Unknown Questions Are Different

A particularly important case is when the user's question cannot be answered from the knowledge base.

For example:

What is the company's health insurance deductible?

The correct response isn't:

"I found the closest document, so I'll make the best guess."

The correct behavior is: The knowledge base does not contain enough information to answer this question.

This distinction is critical in enterprise applications.

A good RAG system should be capable of saying:

No sufficiently relevant context was found.

Problem 5: Relevance Filtering

This is where the simple pipeline needs another stage.

Instead of:

Vector Search
   ↓
Top-K
   ↓
LLM

we can introduce:

Vector Search
   ↓
Top-K candidates
   ↓
Relevance Filter
   ↓
LLM

A relevance filter can use a similarity threshold.

Conceptually:

score >= threshold
    → keep
score < threshold
    → discard

In an initial experiment on a small enterprise handbook dataset, I tested several thresholds.

The results looked like this:

| Threshold | Known-query recall | Unknown-query rejection |
| --------: | -----------------: | ----------------------: |
|      0.20 |               100% |                      0% |
|      0.25 |               100% |                      0% |
|      0.30 |               100% |                     50% |
|      0.35 |               100% |                     50% |
|      0.40 |               100% |                     50% |
|  **0.45** |           **100%** |                **100%** |
|      0.50 |               100% |                    100% |
|      0.55 |               100% |                    100% |

For this initial dataset, 0.45 provided the best separation among the thresholds tested.

That doesn’t mean 0.45 is a universal threshold.

Similarity values depend on the embedding model, corpus, queries, and retrieval setup.

The important lesson is the methodology:

Measure the retrieval behavior and choose the threshold based on evidence rather than intuition.

Problem 6: Retrieval Isn’t the Same as Ranking

Suppose we retrieve 20 candidates.

The retrieval system has done its job:

“Here are 20 potentially relevant pieces of information.”

But we may still want to ask:

“Which five are actually the best pieces of context for this question?”

That’s where reranking comes in.

The distinction is important:

Retrieval

Find a broad candidate set.

10,000 chunks
      ↓
retrieval
      ↓
50 candidates

Reranking

Re-evaluate those candidates and order them more carefully.

50 candidates
      ↓
reranker
      ↓
5 strongest candidates

This gives us a more sophisticated pipeline:

Question
   ↓
Embedding
   ↓
Vector / Hybrid Search
   ↓
Candidate Set
   ↓
Reranking
   ↓
Best Context
   ↓
LLM

Problem 7: Semantic Search Isn’t Always Enough

Embeddings are excellent for understanding meaning.

But enterprise data often contains exact terms that are important:

INC-48271
ERR_CONNECTION_RESET
POL-104
AWS us-east-1
customer_12345

A semantic similarity model may understand the general meaning while missing an exact lexical match that matters.

That’s why another important production pattern is:

Hybrid Retrieval

Combine:

Semantic Search
+
Keyword / Lexical Search

Conceptually:

Question
                    │
          ┌─────────┴─────────┐
          ↓                   ↓
   Semantic Search      Keyword Search
          │                   │
          └─────────┬─────────┘
                    ↓
              Candidate Set

This allows the system to benefit from both:

semantic similarity

and

exact term matching

The Production-Oriented RAG Pipeline

Putting everything together:

Documents
    ↓
Semantic Chunking
    ↓
Embeddings
    ↓
Vector / Hybrid Retrieval
    ↓
Relevance Filtering
    ↓
Reranking
    ↓
LLM
    ↓
Answer + Sources
    ↓
Evaluation + Observability

Now the LLM is no longer sitting directly behind a vector database.

There is an actual retrieval architecture between the user and the model.

The RAG System I Am Building

As part of my ongoing exploration of enterprise AI architecture, I’m building a small RAG system and evolving it step by step.

The current implementation includes:

  • Python
  • FastAPI
  • OpenAI embeddings and LLMs
  • Pinecone
  • heading-aware chunking
  • metadata
  • semantic retrieval
  • configurable top_k
  • similarity filtering
  • source attribution
  • retrieval evaluation

The current pipeline looks like:

Question
   ↓
Embedding
   ↓
Pinecone Retrieval
   ↓
Top-K Candidates
   ↓
Similarity Threshold
   ↓
Relevant Context
   ↓
LLM
   ↓
Answer + Sources

The next step is to experiment with hybrid retrieval and reranking.

That will allow us to compare the baseline retrieval architecture with a more sophisticated production-oriented approach.

How Do We Know a RAG System Is Good?

This is where I think RAG engineering becomes much more interesting.

Instead of simply asking:

“Does the chatbot work?”

we should ask:

Retrieval quality

Did we retrieve the correct information?

Ranking quality

Did the most useful information appear near the top?

Groundedness

Is the answer actually supported by the retrieved context?

Citation accuracy

Do the sources support the claims being made?

Unknown-query handling

Does the system correctly recognize when the knowledge base doesn’t contain the answer?

Latency

How long does retrieval + generation take?

Cost

How much does each query cost?

The result is a much more meaningful engineering question:

Not “Can my RAG application answer questions?” but “Can I measure whether my RAG architecture is reliable?”

Final Thoughts

RAG is sometimes described as:

“Give an LLM access to your documents.”

I think that’s only the beginning.

The real engineering challenge is deciding:

Which information should be retrieved?

Which information should be trusted?

Which information should be passed to the model?

When should the system refuse to answer?

How do we measure whether retrieval is actually working?

The LLM is only one component of that system.

The quality of the final answer depends heavily on everything that happens before the LLM sees the context.

Better context → better answers → more reliable AI systems.

And that’s where production RAG starts to become an architecture problem rather than simply an LLM integration problem.

medium.conteudo_html:
AI security is no longer just about what a model can answer. The bigger question is what happens when that model is connected to tools, credentials, infrastructure and a persistent objective.

Anthropic’s latest report, “Detecting and countering misuse of AI: September 2026,” documents malicious activity observed between December 2025 and August 2026 across cyber operations, influence operations, surveillance, scams, biological misuse, weapons development and illicit model distillation.

I went through the report primarily from an AI/ML and cybersecurity perspective, and what stood out to me was not a single new exploit or a particularly sophisticated prompt.

It was the shift in how AI is being operationalized.

The model is increasingly becoming part of the infrastructure of an attack rather than simply being an assistant sitting in a chat window.

Here are the five things I found most concerning.

1. AI is moving from “assistant” to an actual attack orchestrator

The biggest change is probably the simplest to explain.

Previously, an attacker might ask an LLM: “How do I enumerate this environment?”

Now the model can be placed inside a workflow that actually performs the enumeration, analyzes the results, decides what to investigate next, writes tooling and continues iterating.

Anthropic describes multiple operations where AI was integrated into multi-agent frameworks performing reconnaissance, exploitation and data exfiltration. Humans were still involved, but increasingly at a higher level: defining targets, reviewing results and intervening when necessary.

One case, tracked as GTG-20006, is particularly interesting from a defensive perspective.

The actor had AI-driven workflows covering infrastructure acquisition, phishing, persistence, command-and-control and data exfiltration. More importantly, their agents monitored whether malware was being detected. If a security product detected an implant, the workflow would modify and rebuild it and continue iterating until the detection was avoided.

That creates something close to an adversarial feedback loop:

Deploy
↓
Security product detects artifact
↓
AI analyzes detection
↓
Modify malware
↓
Rebuild
↓
Test again
↓
Undetected?
├── No → Repeat
└── Yes → Deploy

This is fundamentally different from simply using ChatGPT to write malware.

The concerning part is the closed loop.

Traditional security assumes that when defenders create a new detection, the attacker has to spend time and expertise developing a bypass.

AI can reduce that cost dramatically.

Anthropic describes this as potentially “inverting” the cost back onto defenders: detection may no longer slow an attacker down for very long if the attacker can automatically iterate against the detection.

2. The attacker doesn’t necessarily need to understand the target anymore

This one is subtle.

One of the historical barriers in offensive security has been environmental complexity.

A vulnerability might be straightforward, but understanding an unfamiliar organization — its cloud architecture, authentication flows, APIs, internal naming conventions, exposed services and identity relationships — takes time.

The report describes what it calls a form of “vibe hacking.”

The operator provides a high-level objective, such as obtaining access to a particular system or retrieving data. The AI then evaluates the environment, writes scripts, executes them, summarizes the results and continues iterating. The human may not understand every technical detail of the target environment.

That changes the economics of attacks.

Anthropic observed credential discovery across application binaries, repositories, client-side code, container images, metadata endpoints, open storage and even victim-deployed AI agents. One documented operation downloaded 1.8 million Android APKs and scanned them for exposed secrets.

Once a useful credential was found, the workflow could expand access through secret dumps, token amplification, CI/CD injection, database/session dumps and downstream OAuth relationships.

This is where the phrase “security through obscurity” becomes increasingly uncomfortable.

If an organization has some strange internal API, an unusual authentication mechanism or a poorly documented cloud configuration, an attacker historically needed someone who knew how that environment worked.

An AI agent can potentially learn the environment while attacking it.

That doesn’t make every obscure system automatically vulnerable. But it lowers the amount of specialist knowledge required to investigate it.

And that is a very important distinction.

(Before moving on to the 3rd point — checkout my GearRig https://amzn.to/4gS5MSe)

3. Your AI API key is becoming part of the attack surface

This was probably my favorite section of the report from an AI security perspective.

Attackers aren’t just using AI to attack organizations.

They are increasingly attacking the AI supply chain itself.

Anthropic observed attackers stealing API keys and session tokens from legitimate environments and then using them for their own operations. The stolen credentials provide three things simultaneously:

  • Compute — someone else pays for the attacker’s AI workload.
  • Access — the attacker gets access to a capable model.
  • Cover — activity can appear to originate from the legitimate customer.

This creates a new security equation:

Compromised application
↓
Exposed API key
↓
Unauthorized AI access
↓
Attacker gets compute
↓
AI accelerates further attacks
↓
More environments compromised

The interesting part is that AI credentials are no longer merely billing secrets.

They can become offensive infrastructure.

The report describes attackers harvesting API keys from GitHub repositories, applications, Docker containers and other exposed locations. It also documents prompt injection attacks against AI wrapper services such as LiteLLM to extract production API keys from cloud-hosted environments.

From a security engineering perspective, this means AI credentials should be treated much more like production cloud credentials than ordinary application configuration.

Short-lived tokens, scoped permissions, secret scanning, workload identity, key rotation and strong monitoring around unusual API usage are going to matter much more.

4. Agent swarms can turn vulnerability research into a continuous process

This is where things get particularly interesting for people working in offensive security.

Anthropic describes GTG-10007, an operation where AI was used as an engineering and orchestration layer across several parallel workstreams.

One of them continuously performed vulnerability research against security products and network appliances. Another handled reconnaissance. Others focused on malware development and intelligence collection.

The vulnerability-research workflow is the part that caught my attention.

Firmware and binaries were loaded into decompilation tooling. Agents navigated thousands of decompilation calls, formed vulnerability hypotheses, generated exploit code and tested the resulting code against lab copies of the target product. The workflow could then iterate on failed attempts.

Anthropic reports that one continuously running workflow produced more than a dozen possible zero-day findings in a single month.

The important concept here isn’t “AI discovers zero-days.”

It’s parallelization.

A human researcher has finite attention.

An agentic system can have:

Agent 1 → Binary analysis
Agent 2 → Vulnerability hypothesis
Agent 3 → Cross-reference analysis
Agent 4 → PoC generation
Agent 5 → Validation
Agent 6 → Documentation
↓
Shared memory
↓
Next iteration

The report also describes persistent campaign memory, where target lists, credentials, engagement state and instructions survive across sessions.

That’s an important architectural development.

Memory + tools + agents + persistent objectives is a very different threat model from a stateless chatbot.

5. Model theft isn’t just about stealing a model — it’s about stealing capability

The final one is less obvious but potentially very important for the AI ecosystem.

Anthropic describes several illicit distillation campaigns.

Distillation itself is completely legitimate: a powerful “teacher” model generates examples that are then used to train a smaller “student” model.

The problem is industrial-scale unauthorized extraction of another model’s capabilities.

Anthropic reports that attackers created large numbers of fraudulent accounts, used proxy infrastructure and harvested model interactions to reproduce capabilities such as coding, reasoning, data analysis and agentic tool use.

One reported campaign attributed to Alibaba peaked at almost 3 million exchanges per day, using more than 3,500 fraudulent accounts. Across May–July 2026, Anthropic says it observed more than 151 million exchanges associated with that campaign.

But there is a deeper security implication.

A model’s reasoning capability is not confined to one application.

If a distilled model becomes better at general reasoning, coding and tool use, those improvements can transfer to completely different domains — including cyber operations.

Anthropic explicitly notes that its research found distilled models could acquire dangerous capabilities even when the harvested conversations contained relatively little direct material about those domains.

So model extraction is increasingly a capability-transfer problem, not simply intellectual-property theft.

And the attack surface is expanding beyond model weights.

It includes:

  • APIs
  • inference endpoints
  • system prompts
  • tool definitions
  • reasoning traces
  • session state
  • model routers
  • third-party AI applications
  • API keys
  • user conversations

In other words, the AI supply chain is becoming a security boundary of its own.

The bigger picture:

What I found most interesting about Anthropic’s report is that none of these trends exist independently.

They reinforce each other.

Imagine an attacker who obtains a leaked API key.

That key provides access to an AI model.

The model helps enumerate thousands of targets.

Agents analyze the results in parallel.

Another workflow develops tooling.

Another processes stolen credentials.

Another monitors whether defensive controls are detecting the activity.

And persistent memory keeps the entire operation moving between sessions.

That is no longer the classic “attacker + tool” model.

It starts looking more like:

attacker + AI agents + tools + infrastructure + memory + feedback loops.

And that is probably the most important lesson I took from this report.

The security question around LLMs is moving beyond:“Can the model generate malicious content?”

towards:“What happens when the model is given access to the systems required to act on that content?”

That distinction matters enormously.

The model itself might have safeguards. But once it is connected to browsers, terminals, APIs, cloud infrastructure, code repositories and persistent credentials, the system around the model becomes part of the security problem.

For defenders, that means AI security cannot sit in isolation as a prompt-filtering problem.

We need to think in terms of identity, authorization, tool permissions, agent boundaries, telemetry, behavioral detection, secrets management, provenance and continuous monitoring.

The chatbot was only the beginning.

The real security challenge is the agentic system built around it.

medium.conteudo_html:
Trillian Chronicles - Paper #1

“I Swear I Didn’t Write a Single Line: Building a Driving Coach (android) Entirely Through AI”

Series: The Fully AI-Driven Software Development Experiment
Issue: #1 — The Beginning
Date: August 2026
Author: The Human Who Promised Not to Touch the Keyboard (for code, anyway)

“Can AI write a production-grade app from scratch — spec, code, tests, ops — without a human touching the code?”
Nobody knows yet. That’s kind of the point.

Prologue: A Name, A Mission, A Slightly Unhinged Idea

Every great experiment needs a name. This one is called Trillian.

Why Trillian? Because it sounds cool, it’s a bit mysterious, and naming your side project after something sci-fi is basically mandatory at this point. Bonus: it doubles as “Trace McMillan” — fitting for an app that traces you around a racing circuit.

Because what follows is, frankly, a little rad.

The premise: Build a complete, real-world Android application - with a Node.js backend, a PostgreSQL database, Firebase authentication, cloud hosting, and an AI coaching engine — without the human developer writing a single line of code.

Not “minimal code”. Not “mostly AI-generated with a few tweaks”. Zero. Lines. Of. Code. NO IDE installed!

The human’s role is architect, product owner, test oracle, and - when things inevitably go sideways - incident commander. The AI is the developer, the tester, the documenter. The keyboard is for prompts only.

Main Objective: prove that with AI, we will move to next SW System development abstraction layer.

  1. Machine Code to Assembly Language (1940s–1950s)
  2. Assembly to High-Level Languages (1950s–1980s)
  3. High-Level Languages to Managed / Abstract Frameworks (1990s–Present) (…)

Welcome to the Trillian Chronicles!

Chapter 1: What I’m Actually Building?

Before we get into the experiment, let’s talk about what Trillian is.

Phone only Driving Coach is a track day companion app. Picture this: you show up at a racing circuit with your car and your phone. You finger-draw a start/finish line on a map like you’re signing a very sporty cheque. You press record. The app silently captures GPS coordinates and IMU data (accelerometer, gyroscope) at 10Hz throughout your session. You drive. You have fun. You maybe spin once. We don’t judge - the AI coach will, but we don’t.

After the session, the telemetry uploads to the cloud. The backend - a Node.js/TypeScript service - crunches through your GPS track, finds every time you crossed that start/finish line, and reconstructs your lap times. Then it hands everything to Anthropic Claude (yes, an AI coaching the users of an AI-built app — the recursion is intentional), which generates personalised feedback:

“You lost 0.4 seconds braking into Turn 3. Your throttle application in Sector 2 is inconsistent. Your best lap was lap 7 — you were 0.2s faster on the exit of the hairpin.”

Think of it as Strava for track days, with a very opinionated AI in the passenger seat. V1 is post-session only — no real-time coaching, because a push notification saying “BRAKE NOW” at 150km/h is less a feature and more a lawsuit. Future versions could grow into a full social motorsport network. For now: drive, upload, get roasted by Trillian.

117 requirements. 10 fundamental architecture decisions locked before a single prompt was sent to a code generator. Two full test suites. 135 human system acceptance test cases, written to be executed at a real track day.

It’s not a toy. It’s a real system. And it was built - entirely - by humans “driving” AI.

Chapter 2: The Rules of Engagement (or, How to Build Software with Your Hands Tied)

The experiment has three rules. They’re simple. They’re strict. They will occasionally make you (me) want to cry.

#Rule 1: Never touch the code.

The human interacts only through AI. No sneaky edits to a Kotlin file. No “just this once” fix in TypeScript at 11pm. If it’s broken, you write a prompt, file an incident, or invoke an agent. The keyboard is for thinking out loud to a machine - not for patching things manually like a normal person.

#Rule 2: Spec-Driven Development.

Nothing gets built without a specification first. The System Requirements Specification (SRS) is the constitution. Every feature, every API endpoint, every database field traces back to a numbered requirement. UM-01 says registration requires email + password + display name. If the code doesn't implement UM-01, the code is wrong - not the spec. The spec is always right. The spec is basically a deity.

#Rule 3: Test-Driven Development.

Tests are not optional, not an afterthought, and definitely not something you “get around to later.” Unit tests and integration tests are part of every implementation phase. If something breaks without a test catching it first, that’s a process failure, not just a bug. The test suite is the immune system.

Bonus Rule: V-Model.

The classic systems engineering model, dusted off from the 1980s aerospace playbook - requirements define acceptance tests at the top; design defines integration tests in the middle; code defines unit tests at the bottom. All 135 human system acceptance tests for this app were derived directly from the SRS before the app existed. That’s not accidental - it’s the methodology. It’s also slightly terrifying.

Taken together, these rules are, in essence, a wager: can rigorous engineering discipline applied through AI produce reliable software? Can you get aerospace-grade SDLC quality from a chat interface and a well-written spec? We are about to find out.

Chapter 3: The Players

No experiment runs on a single mind. This one used three distinct AI roles, each with a job description that would look great on a business card:

The Architect : Handed a napkin-sketch product idea and told to turn it into a 117-requirement SRS. The human (me) wrote the vision in plain English; the AI wrote the specification with numbered requirements, locked architecture decisions, and enough edge case coverage to make a QA engineer emotional. It thought of things the human hadn’t - like what happens when the Firebase token expires mid-upload at 200km/h. Nobody asked it to think that hard. It did anyway.

The Builder - (Opus family model) : The engine room. Fed the SRS plus a detailed implementation plan (also AI-generated, naturally), it built the Android app phase by phase - scaffold, database layer, telemetry service, backend, UI screens, API client, test suite - across 10 structured phases. Output: ~50 Kotlin files, ~30 XML layouts, ~15 TypeScript files, 61 automated tests. Nobody typed a single fun or class by hand.

The Doctor - RCA Agent (custom .github/agents/): The incident specialist. When things break, this agent steps in with evidence-first reasoning - no "probably" or "in my experience", only "the log shows" and "the stack trace indicates". It is rigorous to the point of being slightly pedantic. That is a feature, not a bug, when you're debugging a SecurityException at 8am on a Saturday. Possible soon will have a child: "Provide Fix Agent" (custom .github/agents/): Agent that will help us provide fix for incidents. most complex agent, will implement the code, runs tests and judge if we can merge the fix.

Chapter 4: The First Incident (crash) - Android 12 Would Like a Word

The app was built. It ran on the emulator. The features were there. The team (one human and a rotating cast of language models) felt quietly smug about this.

Then came the first real test: actually running the recording on a physical device.

Crash. Immediate. Spectacular. Predictable in hindsight, as all crashes are.

java.lang.SecurityException: To use the sampling rate of 0 microseconds,
app needs to declare the normal permission HIGH_SAMPLING_RATE_SENSORS.

Android 12 introduced a rule: if your app samples sensors faster than 200Hz, you must declare HIGH_SAMPLING_RATE_SENSORS in the manifest. The IMU was being sampled at maximum rate (0 microseconds = "give me everything the hardware has, I don't care, I'm a track day app"). The manifest had no such permission. The phone said no, firmly, in the form of a SecurityException.

The human’s instinct — forged by twenty years of muscle memory — was to open the manifest file and add one line. Three seconds. Done. Coffee still warm.

Rule 1 says no. Put the keyboard down.

So instead: incident report filed in 03_incidents/, RCA agent invoked, root cause confirmed with evidence, fix prompt written, fix applied by the AI, build verified. The whole loop took considerably longer than three seconds.

But here’s the thing. What it produced was: a documented incident with root cause, evidence chain, fix, and a prevention note — all traceable back to the SRS non-functional requirement that the app must sample at minimum 10Hz. Six months from now, when someone asks “why is HIGH_SAMPLING_RATE_SENSORS in the manifest?", the answer is sitting in the repo with its full paper trail.

The three-second fix would have left nothing. The process-compliant fix left institutional memory.

That is the whole trade. Slower in the moment, richer forever.

Chapter 5: Scoreboard — End of Sprint Zero

As of June 2026, here’s the honest state of the mission:

  • DimensionStatusSRS (117 requirements) — ✅ Approved, locked
  • Android App Build — ✅ Builds successfully
  • Backend Build -✅ Builds successfully
  • Unit Tests (61) -✅
  • PassingHuman Acceptance Tests (135) — ✅
  • Documented, ready for execution
  • Real device testing — ⚠️ One crash found, one crash fixed
  • Track day validation🔜 Pending

The app runs. The features are there. The overall verdict was “surprisingly good” — which is a genuinely surprising thing to say about a codebase no human ever typed. Or maybe not surprising at all. The spec was precise. The plan was structured. The AI followed instructions.

The lesson from Sprint Zero, stated plainly: AI code quality is a direct reflection of spec quality. Vague prompt → vague result. Clear, complete, well-reasoned spec → something you can actually run, test, and demo. The AI is not magic. It’s a very fast, very literal contractor. Write good requirements, get good code.

Chapter 6: The Questions We’re Here to Answer

This paper is the first in a bi-monthly series. Each issue tracks the experiment’s progress — what worked, what blew up, what was learned. The open questions driving the whole adventure:

  1. Can a fully spec-driven, AI-implemented project stay quality without a human ever patching the code?
  2. Does the V-Model survive contact with AI-generated code? Early sign: surprisingly yes — because spec-driven AI code is paradoxically more traceable than a lot of human-written code.
  3. How far can AI agents carry operations? RCA, incident triage, fix generation — can the human stay out of the repo even when the production system is on fire at 2am?
  4. What does this process actually cost? Not in euros — in time, in prompt iteration, in cognitive effort. Is it faster than traditional development? Probably not. Is it more disciplined? Possibly. Is it more fun? Absolutely.
  5. Is this the future, or an elaborate way to make simple things hard?

Honest answer right now: we don’t know. The app builds. One real crash was caught and fixed without human code intervention. The system tests are waiting for a track day with tarmac and tyre squeal. There is a lot of road left in this experiment.

But what we can already say: a complete, working application — real architecture, real tests, real operational tooling — was built entirely from a specification document, by AI, with a human who never touched the source. That’s not nothing. That is, in fact, the entire point.

Epilogue: Mostly Working

The Trillian project’s current official verdict on fully AI-driven software development: “Mostly working.”

That’s a better grade than most side projects get. We’ll take it. For now.

Paper #2 will cover the first real track day — GPS accuracy in the wild, lap detection quality on actual tarmac, and whether the AI coaching feedback is genuinely useful or just very confidently wrong. Given what’s been delivered so far, the bet is on “surprisingly useful.” We have been surprised before. Pleasantly.

Until then: write the spec, trust the process, and for the love of all things engineering —

Do. Not. Touch. The. Code.

I Spent Weeks Building AI Skills Inside a Chat Window.

Here’s What Nobody Tells You About It.

A real story about building six connected AI skills entirely through conversation — the mistakes that shaped them, the day it almost disappeared, and what actually happens when a team asks: can everyone use this?

There’s a particular kind of dread that comes with opening a real RFP for the first time. Not the summary slide someone made for the kickoff call. The actual document: four hundred pages, split across a main body and a “detailed requirements” appendix that contradicts the main body in three places you won’t find until it’s too late. Somewhere in there is an application inventory, a spreadsheet with names like “eSuite/TIPS/QDOD” and “Aligne Registration,” and no column that reliably tells you which of those four hundred systems a real customer would ever touch, and which ones just move data around in the dark.

Next to that sits the incident data. Not one file, several, from different systems that don’t agree on what a “ticket” even is. One export calls something a Bug. Another calls the same kind of thing an Incident. A third has no type field at all, just a description and a date.

Somebody has to turn all of that into a staffing number, a price, and a leadership deck, by Thursday.

I spent a stretch of my working life doing exactly that, not once but as a repeating pattern, pursuit after pursuit, and at some point I stopped doing it by hand and started building something to do it with me. Not a script. Not a model I trained. A set of AI skills, built entirely inside a chat window, in plain English, over the course of dozens of conversations. This is the story of building that thing, breaking it, watching it break in ways I didn’t expect, and, more than once, catching a mistake right before it would have shipped.

Where it actually started: one skill, and a keyword list that lied to me

The first thing I tried to build was the simplest-sounding piece: read an RFP, read an application list, and tell me which applications were customer-facing. I figured a keyword list would get most of the way there — anything with “portal,” “customer,” “CRM” in the name, flag it.

It didn’t work. Not a little bit off. Genuinely wrong, on nearly half the real rows I tested it against. A payment-processing backend with no login screen anywhere near it turned out to be squarely customer-facing, because it was the exact system charging real people’s credit cards in real time. A tool literally named “Customer Nomination Portal” turned out, once I actually read what it did, to be nothing a customer ever touched. The name lied. The keyword list, trusting the name, lied right along with it.

That was the first real lesson, and it shaped everything after it: never classify anything from a label alone. Read the actual content. If the content doesn’t tell you enough, go look it up. If you still can’t tell, ask a human rather than guess and hope. I wrote that rule into the skill’s own instructions, in plain language, the way you’d write a note to a new colleague on their first day. And because it was instructions rather than code, I could watch it work — or fail — in real time, in the same conversation, and just… fix it. Rewrite the paragraph. Try again.

Six skills need a conductor

One skill turned into two, then six: one to classify the applications, one to read incident tickets and figure out how much of that work needed frontline triage versus deep specialist attention, one to turn that into an actual staffing estimate, one to price the commercial structure around it, one to research the client’s business and technology posture, and one to assemble everything into a single, leadership-ready brief.

Six skills that each did one real thing well immediately created a new problem: something had to decide which one ran when, in what order, and what to do if a step revealed something the plan hadn’t anticipated. That became the seventh piece — an orchestrator — and it does five real jobs, none of which is the actual work itself:

It validates — reads every file that gets uploaded, all the way through, not just the filename or the first column, before deciding what kind of data it’s actually looking at.

It plans — states the whole sequence of steps up front, in plain language, and waits for an actual yes before doing anything.

It gates — runs one step, watches what comes out of it, and only then moves to the next. If a step’s own internal question needs answering, the orchestrator doesn’t answer it on the user’s behalf just because the plan was already approved.

It produces — makes sure every artifact each step is supposed to generate actually gets generated, rather than quietly skipping the parts nobody explicitly asked to see again.

And it learns — when a real correction comes in, it writes that correction permanently into the right skill’s own file, not just into the current conversation, so the next run doesn’t repeat the same mistake.

Here’s the detail that took me a while to really sit with, and it’s the most honest thing I can tell you about how this actually works under the hood: none of that coordination happens through code calling code. There’s no function signature, no schema, no return value passed between the orchestrator and the classifier and the pricing skill. What actually happens is that one skill’s instructions contain a sentence that says, in effect, “go read this other skill’s own file, and follow what it says.” The model reads that sentence, fresh, every single time, and does exactly that. That’s the entire mechanism. Instructions calling instructions, held together by a model’s ability to read and follow them correctly, over and over, under real pressure, with real data.

Once you see that clearly, you stop thinking of this as “software” in the traditional sense. It’s closer to a very well-organized set of standard operating procedures, handed to someone extremely capable, extremely fast, and, this part matters, not always right the first time.

The part that actually took the longest: teaching it to catch its own mistakes

Building six skills that each technically worked was the easy part, in hindsight. The real work came after: running the pipeline against real, messy, contradictory data and finding the places where “technically correct instructions” still produced a wrong answer.

Two moments stand out, because they taught the same lesson twice, in two different disguises.

The first: a file’s own resolver-team field showed nothing but generic integration-team names, nothing that looked remotely connected to the specific system I was trying to analyze. On the strength of that one field, the natural move was to conclude the file was irrelevant and set it aside. Instead, I made myself read the actual ticket descriptions inside it. Buried in the free text, the exact system I was looking for was named, not once but hundreds of times, in job names and error messages that never showed up in any structured column at all.

The second, a few steps later: a different file’s own “type” field read as one specific kind of record, entirely, nothing else. Trusting that field would have meant treating the whole file as the wrong kind of data and excluding it. Reading the actual titles instead, the overwhelming majority of them carried a real, verifiable ticket number belonging to the exact record type I actually needed. The field was describing something else, which tool had logged it, not what it actually was.

Same lesson, twice: a structured field tells you how something was labeled by whoever filled it in. It doesn’t tell you what the thing actually is. The only way to know that is to read it.

What made this feel less like “using a tool” and more like mentoring someone was what happened next. I didn’t just fix the immediate problem and move on. I wrote the pattern — not the specific client details, just the shape of the mistake — permanently into that skill’s own instructions, as a named, generalized lesson: check the filename, check every column, read real content, before you decide a file doesn’t matter. The next time this pipeline runs, on a completely different pursuit, it starts already knowing not to make that exact mistake. That’s not a metaphor. That’s a paragraph of English, sitting in a file, that gets read into context every time the skill triggers.

Getting smarter has a real cost, and nobody tells you that part upfront

Here’s where I want to be honest rather than triumphant, because the honest version is more useful.

The mechanism for “getting smarter over time” in a system like this is, almost entirely, writing more into the instructions. Every lesson learned becomes another paragraph, another reference file, another thing the model has to read the next time the skill triggers. That’s not free. Across the life of this project, the working conversation eventually grew large enough that it needed to be compacted, summarized and compressed, just to stay usable. The system’s entire memory of its own history, at a certain point, became too heavy to carry around in full.

That’s a genuine trade-off, not a bug. The same mechanism that makes the system more careful over time also makes every future conversation start a little heavier. Nobody selling you on “AI that learns from its mistakes” mentions that the learning itself has a storage cost, paid in the currency of context, but it does, and it’s worth knowing before you build something the same way.

There’s a second, separate kind of memory worth naming, because it’s a genuinely different mechanism and it’s easy to conflate the two. Alongside the skill files themselves, a lightweight memory of past conversations can persist across sessions: a running sense of who you are, what you’re working on, what you’ve already told the system, carried forward without you having to repeat it. That’s not the same thing as a lesson written permanently into a skill’s own instructions. One is “the system remembers this specific fact about this specific situation.” The other is “the system now permanently behaves differently for everyone, forever.” Getting those two confused is an easy, costly mistake: treating a passing conversational note as if it were a permanent, generalized fix, or the reverse.

The day it almost disappeared

Somewhere past the halfway point of building this, I asked for a full backup — a zipped archive of every skill file, just to have a copy saved somewhere outside the working environment. It felt like a small, slightly paranoid ask at the time.

A while later, in a completely different working session, I went looking for those same skills and found four out of fourteen. The other ten, including the orchestrator itself and two of the six pipeline skills, were simply gone. Not corrupted. Not moved. Gone, the way a folder is gone after a machine gets wiped and rebuilt from a clean image, which is more or less exactly what had happened underneath, invisibly, between one working session and the next.

The backup zip, asked for on a hunch weeks earlier, was the only surviving, verified-complete copy of that work. I didn’t just trust that it existed. I opened it, extracted every file, and read the actual content back out before restoring anything, because “the zip file is the right size” and “the zip file actually contains what you think it contains” are two different claims, and I’d rather find out the hard way in a sandbox than the harder way in front of a client.

The lesson here isn’t subtle: whatever environment you’re building this kind of thing inside, don’t assume it’s a permanent home. Treat every meaningful piece of work as something that needs a real, verified copy living somewhere else, before you need it, not after.

The question that seemed simple: “can the whole team actually use this?”

Once the pipeline worked, the obvious next question arrived: this is genuinely useful — how does everyone else on the team get to use it, from inside the same chat interface, without each person needing their own separate copy of six skill folders sitting in their own individual environment?

My first answer was wrong, and I want to walk through exactly how, because the correction is more instructive than the original idea.

There’s a real, well-documented way to package multiple skills into a single, versioned, installable unit — a manifest file, a folder structure, a marketplace you can point at and install from with a single command. I researched it properly, checked the actual technical requirements against the real skill files, confirmed nothing would break in the process, and wrote out a complete, step-by-step plan for building it.

It was a good plan for the wrong tool. That entire packaging mechanism belongs to a developer-facing, command-line version of this technology — built for someone working from a terminal on their own machine, not for a team collaborating inside a shared chat interface. The two are genuinely separate systems: skills built for one don’t automatically show up in the other, and nothing about installing a package on a command line puts anything into a chat window at all. I’d built a complete, technically correct answer to a question nobody had actually asked.

There’s a real difference underneath that mistake worth pulling apart, because it’s not just “two systems with different plumbing” — it’s two different ways of actually building the thing in the first place, and they suit different people doing different jobs.

A skill built through a command-line tool is written the way software is normally written: someone opens a file, writes instructions, saves, tests, commits. It rewards someone comfortable in that environment, and it’s genuinely well-suited to a developer maintaining a tool for other developers.

Everything in this piece happened the other way. Every one of these six skills was written, argued with, broken, and rewritten entirely in natural language, inside the same chat window where the actual work was happening — often in the middle of a real task, the moment a real mistake surfaced. There was no separate “build” step and “use” step. The fixing happened in the same breath as the failing. For the actual audience this was built for — analysts, consultants, and reviewers who think in RFPs and staffing models, not in pull requests — that’s not a lesser way of building something. It’s the only way that audience would ever have built it at all. The command-line version demands you already be a developer before you can start. The chat-native version only demands that you can describe, clearly, what went wrong and what should happen instead — which is a much larger group of genuinely capable people.

That’s the real argument for why this way of building suits enterprise chat users better, not just differently: it puts the ability to fix the system in the hands of the people who actually notice when it’s wrong.

The real answer, once I went looking properly, was already sitting inside the chat platform itself: on team and organization plans, a skill you’ve built can be shared directly — with specific colleagues, with a defined group, or with the entire organization — and it shows up in each recipient’s own skills list, right inside the same chat interface everyone already uses, no terminal, no installation step, no separate packaging format required. Upload once. Share it. Everyone toggles it on. Update it later, and everyone using it gets the update automatically, without doing anything themselves.

That’s the version worth knowing about if you’re trying to bring something like this to an actual team of people who live in a chat window all day, rather than a command line. It’s less impressive-sounding than “install our custom plugin marketplace.” It’s also the one that actually reaches the people you built this for.

What this actually proves

I don’t think the takeaway here is that AI is about to replace anyone doing this kind of work. What I watched happen, across dozens of real conversations, was narrower and — to me — more interesting: six connected pieces of plain-English instruction, built and refined entirely through natural conversation by someone who never wrote a line of application code, correctly handled a genuinely complex, high-stakes, real piece of work. Hundreds of real applications, classified correctly on evidence rather than assumption. Thousands of real support tickets, read and understood well enough to catch two of its own file-reading mistakes before they became wrong numbers in a real deliverable. A staffing estimate, a commercial structure, and a leadership brief, assembled from real data, with every gap named honestly instead of quietly filled in with a plausible-sounding guess.

It’s also, genuinely, still young. The coordination between skills is held together by prose being read correctly, not a guaranteed contract. Getting smarter costs real context weight. The environment it runs in isn’t guaranteed to remember what you built inside it, unless you go out of your way to make sure it does. None of that is a reason to dismiss it. It’s the actual, honest shape of what building with this looks like right now — worth knowing precisely, rather than either oversold or waved away.

I’d rather tell you both halves of that than just the part that makes a better headline.
